idiom_name: struct field 'bool dirty' plus a cached derived member, recomputed in a guarded accessor
implementation_notes: The pattern is entirely hand-written: a struct carries the primary data, the cached derived value and a bool (or bit-field) dirty marker; every mutating function sets the marker, and the accessor recomputes when it is set and clears it afterwards. C offers no properties, no member accessors and no inheritance hook, so the invariant lives in convention - document the marking rule at the top of the header and keep every mutator next to the accessor it must mark. The only language primitive for the flag itself is the atomics library: `_Atomic _Bool`/`atomic_bool` with atomic_load/atomic_store from <stdatomic.h> is required when the struct is shared across threads, while a plain bool suffices single-threaded. Do not reach for `volatile` as a substitute - it orders nothing and provides no atomicity.
pitfalls: Nothing enforces the invariant: a mutator that forgets `dirty = true` compiles cleanly and leaves the cache stale, and because there is no encapsulation the marking code is duplicated across every function that touches the struct.

Copying the struct (assignment, memcpy, passing by value) copies the flag together with the cache, but any pointers inside the cached value still point into the source object - rebuild after a copy or mark the copy dirty.

Sharing the struct across threads needs atomic_bool/_Atomic _Bool with atomic_load/atomic_store; a plain bool written by one thread and read by another is a data race and the compiler may keep the value in a register.
A 'clean' flag in a struct that is also serialised to disk or sent over the wire needs an explicit on-the-wire convention (the flag is derived state, not data); recompute it after deserialisation.
